## Overview

The package exposes one user-facing function, `predict`. It predicts ammonia emission dynamics following fertilizer application. The model is a recurrent neural network trained on the ALFAM2 database (Hafner et al., 2025). See [here](model_description.html) for a full description of the model.

This guide covers the three most common workflows:

1. predicting from plot-level data only;
2. supplying a custom time and weather table;
3. comparing several application scenarios.

## Import the package

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from nh3pred import predict
```

## Minimal prediction

`pdat` contains one row per field application. The `id` column uniquely identifies each application and links it to optional time-dependent data.

Only the variables needed to describe this example are supplied below. All other variables are completed with package defaults.

```{python}
pdat = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "id": [1],
        "tan_app": [70],
        "app_method": ["bc"],
    }
)

predictions = predict(pdat)
```

When `idat` is omitted, predictions use cumulative times 2, 4, and then four-hour intervals from 4 to 48 h, and twelve-hour intervals from 48 to 240 h. The package uses a repeating default daily temperature and wind profile and assumes no rainfall.

```{python}
predictions[
    [
        "id",
        "ct",
        "air_temp",
        "wind_2m",
        "prediction_erel",
        "prediction_ecum",
    ]
].head()
```

## Plot the prediction

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(
    predictions["ct"],
    predictions["prediction_ecum"],
    color="#0072B2",
    linewidth=2,
    label="Prediction",
)
ax.set(
    xlabel="Time since application (h)",
    ylabel="Cumulative ammonia emissions (kgN-NH3/ha)",
    title="Predicted ammonia emissions over time",
)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Supply custom time and weather data

`idat` contains one row per application and time point. Time points may be irregular. In this example, air temperature is supplied while wind and rainfall are omitted.

```{python}
idat = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "id": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
        "ct": [2, 8, 20, 32, 48],
        "air_temp": [16, 21, 13, 15, 18],
    }
)

custom_predictions = predict(pdat, idat)

custom_predictions[
    ["id", "ct", "air_temp", "wind_2m", "rain_rate", "prediction_ecum"]
]
```

Supplied application values are retained unless a documented completion rule applies. All numeric output columns, including times and weather, are rounded to two decimals; calculations use full-precision inputs. A missing `air_temp` or `wind_2m` column is filled by interpolating the corresponding default profile at the requested `ct` values. An absent rainfall column defaults to zero. Missing values inside a supplied weather column are not filled with the default weather profile.
Because public predictions represent micrometeorological measurements,
`wind_2m` is routed internally to the model's micrometeorological wind input.

## Compare several scenarios

Each row of `pdat` may describe a different scenario. Here, three otherwise identical applications differ only in application method.

```{python}
scenario_pdat = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "id": [1, 2, 3],
        "tan_app": [70, 70, 70],
        "app_method": ["bc", "ts", "os"],
    }
)

scenario_predictions = predict(scenario_pdat)

scenario_predictions.groupby("id", as_index=False).tail(1)[
    ["id", "ct", "app_method", "prediction_ecum"]
]
```

See the [scenario comparison vignette](scenario_comparison.html) for a complete visual comparison.

## Control computation time

```{python}
#| eval: false
predictions = predict(
    pdat,
    idat,
    batch_size=128,
)
```

- `batch_size` controls how many application sequences are processed together.
  Larger values may improve speed but require more memory.

## Next steps

Consult the [input reference](input_reference.html) for accepted columns, default values, and input conventions. Predictions outside the ranges represented in the training data should be interpreted cautiously.
